speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of urgent and pressing necessity under the terms of Standing Order 43.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION TO ENSURE SAFETY IN TRANSPORTATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to seek the unanimous consent of the House to put forward a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
I believe it is imperative that new regulations to protect the public from accidents caused by the transporting of dangerous, toxic and explosive materials in an unsafe manner be presented immediately. Dozens of accidents on our railways could cause disruption and create extreme danger for members of the public anywhere in Canada, as was the case for 250,000 people in Mississauga last weekend. An inquiry by the Canadian Transport Commission will not be able to ensure more than a public hearing. I would, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow):

November 14, 1979
That to avoid delay, the Minister of Transport refer to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications the matter of hot box detectors, the separation of dangerous commodities and the proper identification of all containers as to contents and risk to persons, with instructions to recommend amendments to ensure safe transportation of such dangerous products and prepare legislation for speedy passage at the earliest possible date.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion concerning a significant and urgent matter.
The prefabricated homes industry represents 25 per cent of the single-family home construction industry in Canada, and in Quebec, in 1978 alone 36 plants produced a shipping value of $83 million and employed almost 1,500 workers. Following the excessive interest rate increase ordered by the present government, 50 per cent to 60 per cent of orders have been cancelled or delayed, which will mean the closing of 50 per cent of those plants and the lay-off of two-thirds of the workers. That this House instruct the government to act immediately to help industries which must go out of business and reduce the effects on the Canadian economy of the economic policies it has implemented until now and that result in an increasing number of lay-offs and higher unemployment rates in the country.

MRS. APPOLLONI-ANSWER GIVEN BY MINISTER OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a question of privilege and thank you for giving me the opportunity, one which I do not take lightly and which I assure you I shall not abuse either through length or content of intervention.
I intend to centre my presentation on two main points, both of which concern the derailment of the CP freight train which occurred at midnight on Saturday, November 10.
At 7.02 a.m. on Sunday, November 11, CKO All News Radio in Toronto reported that chlorine was leaking from one of the tank cars. A similar report was made by Newsradio of Ottawa at 7.15 a.m., and was confirmed by CKOY Ottawa at eight o'clock on Sunday morning. Reports of the chlorine leak were also carried by CBC, CTV and Global on Sunday, over their respective television stations. Monday newspapers, including the Montreal Gazette, The Toronto Sun, The Ottawa Journal and The Citizen-to mention only a few-all reported a chlorine leak. The early edition of The Globe and Mail of November 12 specified, on page 10, that "between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. chlorine gas was discovered leaking from a derailed tank car".
At 2.30 on Monday afternoon, sir, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie) what specific steps were being taken to protect the people of Mississauga and of neighbouring communities from possible chlorine vapours arising from the leakage. The minister's reply, as reported at page 1182 of Hansard, was:
Mr. Speaker, certainly I would not want to give any comfort to the suggestion of a rumour that there is a leak.
Some rumour! I should point out that in an effort to be fair to the minister, lest I had heard him incorrectly, I went upstairs to check the Hansard blues but was advised I could not cite the rough copy in the House. The minister had a further opportunity to correct his statement at the end of the question period but chose not to raise a point of order, so as to do so. It was then, sir, that I rose on a point of order and asked leave to be recognized on a question of privilege, later postponed until the minister's return to the House.
My first point, then, is that by his cavalier dismissal of confirmed reports 1 have documented from reputable news agencies, as mere rumour, the minister not only damaged their credibility but seriously impugned my integrity and that, by denying the premise of my question, he effectively obstructed me from representing the deep and legitimate concerns of my constituents.
Concern for my constituents and, indeed, for all the people of Canada, brings me to the second phase of my question of privilege, because when referring to the leak, the minister went on to say "I have no such knowledge of that." I would remind the House that confirmed reports show that the leak occurred between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. on November 11, yet some 36 hours after the accident occurred, and despite several well-publicized

November 14, 1979

reports, the minister glibly informed the House that he had no knowledge of what, but for the grace of God, could have been the most serious threat to health and even life that Canadians have faced since the First World War.
Mr. Speaker, my honour and credibility as a member of Parliament have been seriously questioned by the minister, but I suggest that the broader threat posed by this incident is to the confidence the people of Canada can place in this minister and his advisers. 1 therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery):
That this entire matter be brought before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

So I can assure the hon. member and anyone else who is interested in the matter that I was well aware of the leak.
1 heard the hon. member's question. She used the words "I gather there already is". I thought she was referring to a second leak. My concern was not to give any credibility to the suggestion there was another leak, because anyone who has been involved at any time in an evacuation operation knows that one of the greatest enemies of evacuation is panic.
My assumption was that the hon. member was talking about another leak. Clearly, anybody who was in the country knew that there was a first leak. I was in Mississauga and, as I say, there were members of my own family being evacuated, so I was clearly aware of a leak. It appears when I read the blues that the hon. member was clearly not talking about a second leak, but that was the way I took the question. Certainly as I read the blues I can understand her concern, and I hope she will accept my apology in the matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early in the question period today the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) asked a question of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) referring to the Canadian Transport Commission. He said in part, "Is the commission being forced to reduce its already inadequate staffing by 100 people at a time when it requires more people to do its job, not fewer?" Immediately following his question I rose to ask a supplementary. When you did see me, Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board had left the House, so I suggested that perhaps you might see me again when he returned, which you generously did, and I put what I thought was a very straightforward, direct, and important question, asking directly whether in fact the Canadian Transport Commission had suffered a reduction in man-years as a

result of government cutbacks. For some reason I was cut off by Your Honour.
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure you that I was in no way trying to flaunt the procedures of the House, and I ask for your guidance in respect to what manner my question offended the procedures of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member will realize, of course, that he had asked a question supplementary to the one just discussed. He clearly rose just after or during the question by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Epp). He used the word "supplementary" when he got to his feet which, whether I was wrong or not, left clear the impression that he was trying to ask a supplementary on that question to that minister and on that subject. When I recognized him, he moved to a different subject.
If I am to follow the practice, as I did in this case, 1 had him on the list of questioners and would have recognized the hon. member for his own question on his own. I accelerated his position because he indicated to me that he had a supplementary question. When a member rises in his place and uses the word "supplementary" to the Chair, that to me means that it is supplementary to the question just dealt with, and if I tried to treat it any other way, it could be chaotic.
The hon. member was attempting to put a question which was supplementary to the very first question asked in the question period, and if I were to allow all members to use that way of getting recognized during question period, I could not keep any kind of order at all. I have to take "supplementary" in that way to mean supplementary to the question which is on the floor at the present time, and I therefore break up the expected rotation to go to a member to follow the same subject. If it is not on the same subject that is on the floor, the results can be chaotic and, I think, unfair to members. For that reason I did not let the hon. member put his question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the debate was under way in committee yesterday, there were a series of questions posed for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources by certain members. The minister had to leave to attend a conference, and I sat in for the latter part of those questions.
First 1 should like to advise the committee that the questions of the members posed when the minister was in attendance will be answered in writing to the particular members and, in particular, the question posed by the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle will be answered directly by the minister. The questions I should like to answer were those posed by the hon. member for Regina East, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre, and the hon. member for Edmonton East.
I should like to start first with the questions posed by the hon. member for Regina East. At the opening of his statement the hon. member asked if the reason the federal government was able to keep oil prices down was because the government had made some kind of a deal to compensate the province of Alberta through gas exports. The answer to the question is, categorically, no. Oil pricing is a matter of national concern. Hon. members are aware that a first ministers' conference took place earlier this week and that a meeting is now taking place between the Prime Minister, my minister, and representatives of the producing provinces. That meeting is taking place this week. The procedure will be for the price of oil to be set through that process.
With respect to the price and the quantity of gas exports, that is a matter for the National Energy Board. The National Energy Board will make its decision on findings as to the amounts of natural gas which are reasonably surplus to Canadian needs and based on finds and capped reserves within the gasfields.
Then the hon. member for Regina East raised a series of other questions concerning the use of insulation within homes in Canada as part of the conservation program. He questioned the safety standards that were being used for insulation or some types of insulation materials for houses. In particular I
November 14, 1979

advise the committee that cellulose insulation products are now regulated under the Hazardous Products Act. Standards have been set by the Canadian government specification board. There is regulation of the manufacture of these products which is now administered by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. His concern with respect to safety standards, while I appreciate it being raised, is one that has been met by the government.
Then the hon. member went on to suggest that four policies should be adopted with respect to the insulation program. He suggested that the first policy should be adequate research. I should like to advise the member that research in this area is a responsibility of the National Research Council, in its division of building research, which has an ongoing program specifically related to energy conservation. It has a current operating budget of about $2.5 million for research in this area. In addition, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has an ongoing supportive research program under CANMET, the Canadian Centre for Mineral and Energy Technology. Under a division of CANMET, the division of Canadian combustion research laboratories, a further research program on the effectiveness of insulation is being carried out.
The second question or head the hon. member posed had to do with proper regulation. The federal government is a leader with respect to regulation. It adopted a national building code which it urges all provinces to adopt. The jurisdiction for the adoption of the building code lies with the provinces. However, the federal government has taken the lead. Also I should advise the hon. member that the national building code subcommittee's "Measures for Energy Conservation in Buildings," a recently published additional document, sets out even more stringent standards which are now being urged upon provincial governments.
Also the hon. member suggested that the program should cover more than just insulation of roofs and walls. I should like to advise the member that the program now covers in addition to insulation, caulking, weatherstripping and vapour barriers. For consideration in the future will be improvements to doors and windows.
His suggestion was that the program should not be turned over to the provinces, with funding by the federal government. However, his fourth point was that the entire program should be personalized and should use community facilities. It is for that reason the program is being turned over to the provincial governments. The provincial governments, and local municipalities under provincial government auspices, have inspection programs, training programs, all the training programs for installers and builders. All licensing programs are under the jurisdiction of the provinces. It is within the provincial jurisdiction that the most effective control can take place.
There is a failing in the program which we recognize, and that is that rental accommodation is not being upgraded. Neither the landlord nor the tenant, because of the term of the tenancy or the tenure in the dwelling, is taking advantage of the program. We have made representations to the provincial jurisdictions for amendments to their landlord and tenants act
Supply
which will bring about encouragement in this particular area. I trust that my comments have answered the questions posed by the hon. member for Regina East.
I should like to turn very briefly to the questions posed by the hon. member for Edmonton East.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is attending a conference at this time which has to do with the question of pricing, a federal government and producing province jurisdiction. I am not certain whether the minister will be back, but I will make inquiries this afternoon and advise the hon. member if it will be possible for the minister to be in the House either tomorrow or Friday, when this matter is being considered in committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Very quickly I should like to respond to the questions posed by the hon. member for Edmonton East and the hon. member for Ottawa Centre. The hon. member for Edmonton East asked if there was a domestic oil supply scenario for 1990. Now, that could be the subject of many hours of debate. However, 1 should like to advise the hon. member that in very short terms the fall in the production of light crude oil is noted and is taking place.
This fall in the production of light crude must be replaced by other sources of energy, and there are only certain other sources of energy. It would be this government's policy to pursue actively the search for all of these sources, and they would include the following: development of heavy oils both in the tar sands and in situ, such as proposed at Cold Lake; enhanced recovery, or research and development into enhanced recovery procedures for the recovery of additional oil from old fields and now producing fields; oil and petroleum products that will come about through new finds, and these finds must take place in the existing Alberta basin and in the frontier regions, which would include both the north and the east coast

November 14, 1979
Supply
areas; production, or if you will, energy consumption also controlled through conservation, and this government will pursue an active program of conservation in all areas of energy use; and lastly, there will be a program of substitution, substitution from petroleum-based products, or oil-based products to gas, biomass and other renewables, the utilization of our coal resources, thermal resources and so on. It will be through a program pursuing all of these areas that we will achieve energy self-sufficiency by the year 1990.
The hon. member also asked if we knew the cost. No, we do not know the cost. We do know, or we can hazard a guess, that in the petroleum area it could cost as much as $100 billion between now and 1990 to become petroleum self-sufficient.
The member then asked where the money would come from. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I have to advise the member that there is no good fairy. Canada is not going to win a world lottery and come up with all of the money. This money is going to have to be earned by Canadians working here; it is through the efforts of Canadians, through their savings, through their industry, through their exports, and through their activities in the world that the money will be raised. It is Canadians who are going to have to raise the money to pay for this. No one else is going to come to our rescue. We must look after ourselves.
The last question was, when do we start collecting the money necessary to pay for this program? Mr. Chairman, 1 would advise that we will start collecting the moment the oil prices are set and the budget comes down. That is the reason we have had the first ministers' conference this week and why there is a conference taking place in western Canada, and why we have budgets. The collection of this money will come about as soon as the Prime Minister returns and announces to this House the policies with respect to the taxation and collection of revenues from the increased prices for oil products.
Lastly I would like to turn to the questions posed by the hon. member for Ottawa Centre. He posed four questions, the first of which was: what price is required to bring on new supplies? It is much the same question as was posed by the hon. member for Regina East, and i hope he will take the same answer. It was put if we had no exact number on the price then we should not embark on this program until we knew the price. I must advise the hon. member that we do not know the price, but the kind of question he posed was one such as, what price to find a cure for cancer; what price to find a cure for poliomyelitis, or what price did we pay for the eradication of smallpox?
We in Canada face a situation which requires action. We as a nation must bear the price, whatever it is, because as a nation we require energy self-sufficiency. With our given resources, with the given knowledge with respect to what we have in the ground in this country, we know that the price is the most reasonable price that can be paid by any industrialized nation in the world.

He also asked what will be the rate of return to the investor for new supplies and, Mr. Chairman, I would advise the member that the rate of return will be the reasonable rate of return for any investor, along with what is required for the activity to take place in this country. The rate of return is something that is now being discussed by the Prime Minister and my minister in their meetings out west, and it is something that has been discussed with the other first ministers, and it will be announced to the House when the program has been set and established. I would have to ask the hon. member to wait until the program is announced by the Prime Minister.
The hon. member also suggested that we could effect conservation by raising prices above world prices. I think the statement he made was that we could dampen consumption by going above world prices; we could dampen consumption to a nil basis simply by raising prices up. That is correct, but it is not reasonable or feasible.
The last question that he asked had to do with the distribution of additional revenues. 1 would again advise the hon. member that the distribution of additional revenues which will accrue to the federal government is for energy self-sufficiency and increased productivity; to finance the goal of being selfsufficient by 1990. The collection of those revenues and the percentages that will be assigned to the various jurisdictions are what are now being negotiated. I would point out to the hon. member that the old program, the program that we have been following since 1975, of a dollar and a dollar every six months, resulted in a surplus in production in 1975 of over 300,000 barrels per day, but a shortfall in November, 1979, of over 314,000 barrels a day, so clearly the old regime was not working and was not bringing us toward self-sufficiency.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I just want to clear up one point. I have just finished reading Hansard of yesterday and the statement that I made, and nowhere in that statement did I ever refer to charging a price to consumers to dampen demand which would be higher than the world price. I said at that time the price to achieve conservation was unknown, and we did not know what it was. It may be higher or lower than the replacement cost. Certainly I never said that consumers in Canada should be charged more than the world price in order to dampen demand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I accept the statement of the hon. member. My notes that I made at the time and my recollection are incorrect. I certainly welcome his statement and suggestion that we should never charge more than world prices.

Mr. Chairman, if I could rise on a similar matter, I would like to clarify that I am not against turning the home insulation program over to the provinces. I did raise some things, however, that I felt a national home conservation program should have, and 1 was concerned that some of those matters would be missing if you just turn it over to the provinces. I think I was making suggestions that allow the provinces to be in, but keep the federal government in as well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I also thank the hon. member for his statement and clarification.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take the opportunity of having the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the House to raise certain questions with her concerning her department and concerning Canadian foreign policy.
I want to begin by publicly repeating the congratulations which I have given the Secretary of State for External Affairs on her appointment, and to promise her that there are many in this party who follow her speeches, statements, and the policies of her department with great interest. Needless to say, I am one of those members who, for personal reasons, has long taken an interest in her department and will continue to do so.
There are basically four areas to which I would like to address myself, and I beg the indulgence of the minister, if 1 may, for a few minutes, to put forward a point of view and then to ask her some questions.
Three really concern peacekeeping and Canada's role, first of all in Cyprus, second of all in the Middle East, and third of all in Rhodesia; and finally 1 have some questions concerning her speeches and the statements by the Minister of Finance concerning Canada's future intentions with respect to foreign aid.
With regard to the Cyprus question, Canada has had a long history of very close involvement in the difficulties of that island since 1963. I would like to put to the minister a slightly different history and conception of the problems on that island from the concept I suspect she is receiving from her department and which, indeed, is American foreign policy and the foreign policy of many of the NATO countries with respect to Cyprus.
There was extraordinary tension between the Greek Cypriot population and the Turkish Cypriot population from before the Zurich agreement in 1960 and the declaration of the republic soon afterwards, all of which is well known to the minister, and it is not necessary for me to go into that. We are dealing with an island that has a population of approximately 600,000 people, of whom over 80 per cent are of Greek origin and about 20 per cent are of Turkish origin. There were a number of internecine and intercommunal problems and problems with respect to the civil rights of the minority, which Canadians have faced in our own history and to which we have found our own constitutional solutions.
There was the dramatic withdrawal by the Turkish Cypriots from the national government in the early 1960s, and a continuing and difficult problem of internal violence which was met by the arrival of the United Nations peacekeeping force in 1964, of which Canada was a member. There was a failure on the part of the population of Cyprus to come to an agreement which would provide for a truly national government. On the one hand there were complaints by the Turkish population that they were a beleaguered minority economically, and were in a more difficult circumstance than the Greek
Supply
majority because they were unable to express their civil rights in a political way and in many cases, they said, to express their religious rights.
On the other hand the majority 80 per cent of the population viewed the island as a whole integral island on which their homes stretched from Kyrenia in the north to Limassol in the south and Paphos in the west, and to which no part of Cyprus was alien to them. There were Greek villages and Turkish villages side by side. Admittedly there was intercommunal violence at times, but there was also a certain amount of intercommunal co-operation and certainly of people living together.
At that time it was the position of the Canadian government that it would do everything it could through advice given by private individuals, our work at the United Nations and our membership in the peacekeeping operation, to attempt to encourage the Cypriots to come to a constitutional solution that would provide for the guarantee of minority rights within the context of a republican government which would apply throughout the island.
Prior to 1974 the difficulties in Cyprus could be described as intercommunal, conflicts between a majority and a minority, which could arise in any country. It was in the summer of 1974 that a dramatic transformation of the difficulties on Cyprus took on an international flavour of far more serious proportions. I am referring to the invasion of the island of Cyprus by the army of Turkey, and the occupation by that army. Indeed, if it were not for the presence of Canadian troops in Nicosia, it, too, would have been occupied by Turkish troops. Were it not for the role which the United Nations played in that incident, there would have been even more and greater violence and conflict then there was.
The net result of the Turkish invasion of 1974 was the occupation of one third or perhaps more of the island of Cyprus, and this resulted in the creation of some 200,000 refugees in a land with a population of 600,000. One-third of the population was rendered homeless, and every single Greek community, with the exception of a small village, was eliminated from the entire northern part of Cyprus and shipped to the south. All Turkish Cypriots living in the southern part of the island were encouraged by the Turkish leadership to leave, and they themselves went to the northern part of the island.
The important part of this history is that whereas before the conflict was of an intercommunal nature within the island of Cyprus between Cypriots, it was now a very different situation. Since 1974 the conflict has been not only between Turkish and Greek Cypriots, but between Turkish troops, Cypriot troops, the government of Turkey and the government of Cyprus which, as the minister knows, is recognized by the Canadian government as a legitimate government for the whole of Cyprus.
Since 1974 there have been a series of proposals and counterproposals from the Turkish side and from the Cypriot side with respect to the political government of the island, the withdrawal of Turkish troops, and the return to a unified country on the island of Cyprus. Since that time Canadian

November 14, 1979
Supply
troops have remained on the island and, indeed, play a critical role in the United Nations peacekeeping force, stationed as they are in Nicosia, which is the hottest point of potential conflict between the two communities. During my visit to Cyprus, and while talking with the commander of Canadian troops there, he made it very clear that the Canadian troops were the linchpin of the military and political operation which the United Nations peacekeeping force is playing on the island of Cyprus.
Cyprus has become not only an international question, but one which involves the policy of the Canadian government. Soon after the election in May, the minister of defence raised publicly for the first time in recent memory the question of the future position of Canadian membership on the peacekeeping force in Cyprus. What the minister had to say concerned me very much because it reflected a popular view of the conflict on the island of Cyprus which, in my view, does not coincide with the facts. The view is that there are two sides and two kinds of Cypriots who cannot get along and, as a result, an intercommunal conflict, and that Canada has been there for so long that really there is no point in our staying any longer because we have become part of the problem, which I think is the phrase used by the minister of defence.
The minister of defence suggested that it might also be better if Canada were to withdraw and let the parties come to whatever solution they would. With all due respect, I think that the minister of defence is confusing the pre-1974 situation with the post-1974 situation. Prior to 1974 one might have understood a certain frustration on the part of the Canadian government with respect to the situation on Cyprus. One might have also understood the feelings behind saying, "This is just an intercommunal conflict. Why should we stay there any longer, and why should we be the good guys in a world made up of bad guys?"
I can understand the natural frustration that a Canadian minister of defence responsible for Canadian troops might feel. After 1974 the minister's description of the situation in Cyprus is a caricature of what is now the real situation. The situation there now is that Turkey, a foreign country, occupies one-third of the island and is supplied with arms by NATO countries, including the United States. Two hundred thousand people have been rendered homeless as a direct result of the Turkish invasion, the government of the island of Cyprus is unable to exercise its authority over one-third of the island, and refugees on the island are completely barred from any communication with any part of their families remaining in the northern part of the island.
The situation on the island of Cyprus may be described as a conflict, not of an intercommunal nature, but as one between the island of Cyprus, the government of Cyprus, and the government of Turkey. It is in that context that I think the situation must be seen.
I know there are those who say we cannot put pressure on the Turks because of NATO, that we cannot put pressure on
[Mr. Rae.)
the Turks because of the importance of maintaining their position in the NATO alliance. This has been the position of the United States government. I would say to the minister, however, that we are facing in the Aegean Sea real conflicts between the Turks and the Greeks which go back a long time.
The answer to the problem in Cyprus must be found. The minister must recognize that the insecurity in Greece itself over the Cyprus issue can easily become just as important as the insecurity in Turkey at the present time. I suggest to her that it is in the interests of the NATO alliance to force Turkey to bargain with the Cypriot government as much as it is in the interests of the alliance to keep this problem alive.
The point of view that I am putting forward-to be quite blunt about it-is that there is no incentive at the present time for the Turkish government to bargain with the Cypriots with respect to the future of Cyprus. Everything is on their side, unless there is incentive. Time is on their side; occupation is on their side; military power is on their side. There is an army of 30,000 Turkish nationals in the north of Cyprus, there is a Greek-Cypriot national guard of 8,000, and a Turkish-Cypriot guard of the same size.
Unless military and economic pressure is put on the Turks to bargain, they have no incentive. They have what they want. They have reached their maximum position. The only thing holding them there is the fact that the NATO alliance, Canada included, has not been able to put pressure on them to reach an agreement with the government of Cyprus that would recognize the principle on the island of Cyprus of a unified island within a constitution that recognizes the legitimate aspirations of all members of the population and that deals directly with the question of the rights of the majority and the rights of the minority.
This may seem like a recondite analysis of a question that is of little concern to many Canadians, but I suggest to the minister that it is an exceptionally important issue. It is a human rights issue, involving a number of refugees; it is an issue involving the continued determination of the Canadian government to recognize its responsibilities and to recognize that there is no easy answer.
The solution of withdrawing the peacekeeping force is, in my view, the easiest solution and also the worst solution to the problem. If Canadian troops are withdrawn, the very future of the peacekeeping force will be placed in doubt. Any remaining pressure on the Turks to negotiate will be diminished. In fact the Turks will be encouraged, because we will be giving credence to their military occupation by withdrawing from our role with the United Nations force. This is a question of critical importance for those many Canadians who are concerned about the future of Cyprus and who recognize that there is, in Cyprus, a problem, not of an intercommunal nature, not an internal problem, but a fight between the government and the army of Turkey and the government of Cyprus.
My specific questions to the minister are as follows, Mr. Chairman. What are the intentions of the government with respect to peacekeeping in December, 1979, and at the six-
November 14, 1979

month renewal date in June next? What discussions and negotiations have taken place between the Government of Canada and the government of Turkey with respect to Turkey's position in presenting proposals? Finally, I would welcome any statement the minister might like to make concerning the situation on Cyprus.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I will ask the other three questions and then let the minister give her complete answer. That is the question with respect to Cyprus, so I will move on to the other three questions. They are much quicker.
With respect to the Middle East, I do not think the minister needs to be told the extent to which we, in this party, have disagreed with the changing positions of the government regarding the relocation of our embassy in Israel. I should like to ask the minister, however, what effect, in her view, the changes that have taken place-quite apart from the economic consequences of the government's decision and then its change of mind-have had on our relations with many Arab countries? What effect have these changes had on Canada's role as a peacekeeping nation in the Middle East? Is there any evidence of our having lost credibility as an important stabilizing force in the efforts of the United Nations, in the Middle East?
My third question also deals with peacekeeping, and concerns Rhodesia. Is the minister in a position to make any kind of statement to the House as a result of the discussions in London, on the potential role that might be played by Canadian troops in Rhodesia, and whether there is any intention to take this step?
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to have an elaboration for the benefit of the House on the meaning of the minister's statements, and those of the Minister of Finance, that we will be concentrating our aid efforts on international winners rather than on international losers and whether we will be tying our international aid efforts-I see the minister shaking her head, so I may have read something between the lines that was not there-and also with respect to her statements that we should begin tying our aid to the political stances taken by Third World countries in the United Nations and elsewhere. Would the minister care to comment on that position? Even if she is shaking her head and indicating that I am misguided, I suspect that is the message that has come from her department to the Canadian people since the election. I think she could clear it up if such is not the case.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member who has just posed those questions to me. 1 recognize very clearly his ongoing personal interest in the external affairs of our country and the work of the Department of External Affairs, and the reason for it. I certainly hope it continues, as I am sure it will. I also recognize that the hon. member has recently had an opportunity to visit Cyprus and make himself personally aware of the situation in that troubled island. I have listened with great interest to his eloquent description of the developments that have taken place over the last few years. I will come quickly to the specific questions he

has posed with regard to Cyprus, to peacekeeping elsewhere, as well as with regard to foreign aid.
As the hon. member said, the Canadian peacekeeping force is situated in Cyprus on a six-month mandate which is renewed every six months, and has been renewed every six months since 1964. We have been there just over 14 years now. The present mandate for our force of 515 military personnel will expire on December 15 of this year. I can assure the hon. member that the mandate will be renewed in another six months.
As the Minister of National Defence has stated, however, and as I have had an opportunity to state on various occasions, the question of when a peacekeeping force ceases to have an active role as peacekeepers, and becomes instead a part of the economy of the area in which it is located, is one that has to be considered. We have been in Cyprus as part of the peacekeeping force for over 14 years. As the hon. member knows, negotiations between the governments most concerned have ceased to be operative in any meaningful way.
It would seem to us that our continuation in a peacekeeping force should be at least partly conditional on the fact that we see some kind of negotiation, some kind of commitment to resolving a problem on the part of those involved, in order to ensure that our ongoing involvement can be contemplated. We have said that in our review of foreign policy and aid policy we will, as well, be taking a look at the whole role of peacekeeping because it is not the intent of this government that our peacekeeping forces stay in a country, or on an island such as Cyprus, without some indication that the problem that has caused them to be there will be tackled by those most concerned.
I have conveyed this, and this was the second question the hon. member posed, directly to the foreign minister of Turkey.
I have made him aware of our concerns because we want to see the negotiations resumed. I have also been in touch with the foreign minister of Greece and conveyed the same concerns to him because I know the influence that Greece would have on the activities of the Cypriot government. For that reason, I hope there can be a resumption of the negotiations which collapsed some time ago.
The hon. member made reference to the fact, and I noted these words, that we should force Turkey to take some action. He used the word "force". I am not sure in what context he used that word. I trust he did not mean in some kind of military context because I would not want to intimate in any way or put forward the proposal that Canada would be engaged in any kind of military intervention that would force Turkey, or indeed the Cypriot government, to return to the negotiating table.
We have used the only forum available to us besides our own bilateral discussions, that is, the United Nations. We have used the United Nations to support resolutions and urge resolutions that this situation be tackled and that some resolve be brought to the problem. We will continue to use the United

Nations as a forum to meet the concerns the hon. member expressed.
The other question the hon. member asked was with regard to peacekeeping in the Middle East. He asked whether Canada's role as a peacekeeper in the Middle East has in any way been diminished in recent months. I can tell him quite straightforwardly that no, it has not. speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member says he toured the Golan Heights as well, so I know he is aware of the very strong commitment that Canada has to it and the very important role we play in that area.
The hon. member asked as well about the situation in Zimbabwe-Rhodesia. As the hon. member and others are aware, discussions are going on at the present time in London arising out of the earlier Commonwealth Conference last summer held in Lusaka. At that Commonwealth Conference the Prime Minister, on behalf of Canada, made it known that Canada would be willing to contribute to any kind of Commonwealth observer group which would be put in place to supervise the elections that would be held in Zimbabwe-Rhodesia.
There has been no approach made to us by the British government to take part in any such activity or, in fact, in any other way in a peacekeeping role. We would have to examine any proposal made to us apart from the one that we already indicated, to help out during the holding of elections. We would have to examine that as to the proposal itself and what it contained, but we have had no request to date in that regard.
I think the hon. member's final question had to do with the government's broad aid policy and what we will be doing. I already indicated in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, and I am sure the hon. member is aware of this, that we are undertaking a full review of aid policy and will be presenting papers on both foreign policy and aid policy to the standing committee, asking them to become the vehicle by which public input is provided to the development of Canada's foreign aid policy for the eighties. I hope he will be a very active member of that committee.
The hon. member made some mention of the fact that he would back winners and not losers. I would like to read for the hon. member's information the countries to which we are extending our aid, the ten countries to which we extend aid in the largest amounts. These countries are Bangladesh, Pakistan, Tanzania, India, Sri Lanka, Tunisia, Zambia, Ghana, Cameroon and Malawi. I leave it to the hon. member to draw his own conclusions as to which countries are being backed with aid policy. In reviewing our aid policy, I trust that we will

face up to some of the questions that in an earlier time may not have been tackled. I am talking now about aid policy with regard to countries which have shown violent abuses of human rights.
The hon. member will be aware that aid to Vietnam has been cut off by Canada. The previous government took that step. We took it further because we believe that the activities in Vietnam, the present expulsion of thousands of Indochinese, the invasion of a neighbouring country, Cambodia-Kampu-chea, with all of the disaster and tragedy that has brought forward, does not in any way elicit our support for a continuing aid program to Vietnam. These are matters which have to be brought up in the light of our aid review.
The same can be said with regard to the question that 1 raised about countries which will not renounce their intention to explode nuclear devices, countries which will not join the non-proliferation treaty but are using their own finances to develop and perhaps explode a nuclear device. These are questions which have to be looked at and should not be avoided when we are tackling our foreign policy review.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I should like to make some comments and raise some questions about Canada's external relations. During the six months since the election, Canada has been without any discernible foreign policy. This would be all very well if one could infer from that that the government had decided to pursue, in broad outline, the directions taken by its predecessor. However, that inference is left in doubt by the questions which the Secretary of State for External Affairs keeps asking. We have no statements of policy. We have only her questions. A question is not a policy. Nor do a series of questions make a policy. I assume of course, that the minister has not consciously adopted her questioning stance as a handy excuse for inaction on the international scene.
The minister has made a virtue of her seemingly endless questions by contending that, in asking them, she has been contributing to a proposed national review of foreign policy. This she offers as a notable innovation in Canadian government practice.
There are two things to be said about the minister's public approach to her heavy responsibilities. One is that Canadians are quite capable of asking their own questions. Canadians are not so inarticulate that they need their minister of external affairs to ask questions about external affairs. What the Canadian public and indeed Canada's allies do need are clear indications of how the government intends to conduct our relations with other countries, whether in international organizations or bilaterally. What Canadians rightly expect of their government is policy, policy on development assistance, on NATO and the UN, on the rich diversity of our relations with other countries. Dressing up a series of questions as a policy will not satisfy the rightful demands of the Canadian people to know what the government intends in an area where our self-interests as a nation, as well as the broad interest of humanity, are so closely engaged.
November 14, 1979

The second thing to be said about the minister's approach is that a foreign policy review is no remarkable innovation. There have been such reviews before, and there will be again. And there is, of course, a continuing discussion in the media, in universities, in churches, in labour unions and in business of Canada's foreign relations, a fact which if the minister did not know it before, she should have learned from her government's foolishness about moving our embassy in Israel. Many Canadians who take part in the lively debate about foreign policy will have been surprised to hear the minister describe it as an "esoteric academic exercise reserved for ivory towers". It is anything but that.
The world in any case moves on, while the minister stands still asking her questions. That is one problem with the government's non-policy in our relations with other nations. Policy must be made, is being made. The minister should by now be able to set forth the broad lines of the policies she must necessarily be pursuing or contemplating.
Another problem with the minister's Socratic stance, as one might call it, is that she raises questions on the one hand of bold new directions while on the other hand she must surely know that there are certain fundamental limitations on Canada's freedom of action in an increasingly interdependent world. Canada is no exception to this inescapable rule of foreign relations. There are certain continua that no Canadian foreign minister can ignore, any more than the foreign ministers of other nations can ignore the particular factors that limit their freedom of action.
Let me offer a few examples with regard to Canada. Bilingualism is basic to Canada. It finds expression in our external as well as our internal affairs. Dividing a continent across the middle has many implications, and history and geography have resulted in an extraordinary complex of relations with the United States. A small population in a large, rich territory must seek prosperity in a high level of export trade, with all that implies, A people so utterly dependent as Canadians on the peaceful international exchange of goods and services dare not lose sight of our vital interest in a structured international community. A nation with long coasts on three oceans must also take a deep interest in international law. Our dolorous progress through two world wars has led Canadians to seek security in collective action, in both the United Nations and NATO. The confluence of our Greco-Judeo-Christian traditions and our Commonwealth and Francophone heritage have produced a nation deeply committed to alleviating the plight of the peoples of less prosperous areas of the world.
These are not deadhand legends, but reality. These, and others, are all fundamental factors in any Canadian foreign policy. The minister observed recently that during the past decade "things have sure changed . . ." In some ways they have, most notably with regard to the many ramifications of oil price increases. But much else has not changed. Many of those immutable elements require discussion now, against the background of the changes that have occurred in other areas. That is another reason why the minister's questions are not policy.
Supply
Let us look for a moment at this need for what we might call a Realpolitik, at a few of the continua I have mentioned, in the hope that at the least the minister may offer a few policy comments on them. Specifically, I want to question the minister about three of these continua: Canada's role in peacekeeping, NATO, and the United Nations generally.
The minister has indicated in a recent statement that Canada will continue to support peacekeeping efforts and will envisage further Canadian participation in such efforts. I was pleased to note this, for Canada's record of support for the United Nations and its peacekeeping activities is a notable one. Canada, in spite of our relatively small size, has participated substantially over the years in peacekeeping efforts, a significant contribution to world security and the peaceful resolution of disputes.
The interests of Canada, an inescapably international country, are best protected by the development of world order and the extension of international rules. These benefits certainly outweigh the costs to Canada of our peacekeeping forces. There are direct costs, of course, over $60 million since 1957; nevertheless we have maintained our commitment to our allies, to the concept of world security and to a world organization devoted to the cause of peace.
I invite the minister to affirm Canada's support for the UN's peacekeeping efforts, including Canada's participation in the Namibia talks and in the disarmament negotiations ongoing at the United Nations.
In the future, it may be that international agreements involving third party verification will offer new opportunities to the UN to monitor disputes in situations short of conflict. A treaty on the law of the sea, for example, could well lead to new means of dispute settlement. Outer space is another subject which will call for new thinking about management and control. Keeping the peace is a flexible concept. Soldiers in uniform are not necessarily an essential part of it. But the skills of the soldier/diplomat are bound to continue to be in demand. Canada will have the personnel to help satisfy some reasonable share of that demand, and will be inclined to do so if the UN provides the conditions for effective operating procedures and adequate political support.
While on the subject of the United Nations' peacekeeping efforts, 1 would also make a more general plea to the minister for support of the United Nations as a whole. She has been very critical of the organization since taking office, unjustly critical. The United Nations certainly has its faults, as any large bureaucratic organization must. To outside observers, the General Assembly may appear to be a forum for futile and emotional debates, dominated by a militantly anti-western, Third World majority. Nevertheless, there is no alternative to the United Nations as a centre of international discussion, information exchange and decision. Canada has long supported not only the active peacekeeping aspects of the United Nations' role but also those aspects of co-operation, consultation, and compromise that can be found throughout the United Nations and in its specialized agencies. The work of these agencies in particular has been invaluable in the tackling of

November 14, 1979
Supply
global problems such as food production, civil aviation, environmental pollution, contagious diseases and population growth. These are critical issues of survival, so successfully managed within the UN system that we take them for granted. They are not to be dismissed as its secondary purpose.
The minister, in her maiden speech to the General Assembly, chose to focus on the weaknesses of the system at the expense of its real strength. In doing so, she cast Canada in the light of a negative, moralizing, and self-righteous critic. The minister is not doing Canada's image abroad any service by adopting such a tone. As a secure and wealthy country Canada can afford more generosity of spirit. We would also be acting more effectively in our long-term interest by encouraging and supporting the world organization. We are not blind to its flaws; their existence does not absolve us of the responsibility to be creative participants in the evolution of the system. Without ignoring problems and shortcomings, we must build on what has been accomplished.
During the post-war years Canada became a major participant in the creation of the world organization, and within that new organization Canada recognized from the beginning its limitations. Nevertheless, Canada soon found the United Nations a congenial, creative place, eliciting any talent for conciliation and harmonization that we may have, a place for maximizing opportunities for the enhancement of both our interests and our status. Whether in collective security arrangements providing Canada with a means of exerting influence on powerful allies or giving substance to diplomatic goals outside the North Atlantic region, or in the corridors lobbying to avoid dangerous confrontations and working with the secretariat, Canadians have done well.
The United Nations is a voluntary system requiring patience and determination and providing a setting for enforced association. We must not weaken the world organization by cynicism, but strengthen the whole network. That means viewing the organization realistically and ridding ourselves of the fantasy that if only self-seeking leaders would get out of the way, mankind could live in sweetness and light.
Along these same lines I would also urge continued support for Canada's long-standing membership in the North Atlantic Alliance. This commitment dates from the period after the second world war when Canada was so active in the international effort to establish a more secure world order and to seek security in collective action. Our participation in the North Atlantic Alliance is important both to ourselves and to our European partners, as a concrete illustration of our determination to contribute to collective security and our participation in the western defence effort.
There are those who have called for Canada's withdrawal from NATO in the mistaken belief that our absence from the alliance would somehow contribute to east-west detente. That detente is more likely to be found in the SALT agreements, disarmament initiatives and, indeed, in the broader field of economic co-operation. In any event, such a withdrawal would,

among other things, ignore the value to Canada of Europe as a counterweight to omnipresent United States influence. In a sense, our membership in NATO represents a calling in of the old world to redress the imbalance of the new.
I should be pleased to have comments from the minister about our continuing commitment to the Atlantic alliance and her thoughts about what form that commitment will take in the future.
I have already said that a curious feature of the government's approach to foreign affairs is what sometimes seems to me to be endless questioning. Perhaps the Canadian people and our allies would not have become weary of the minister's questions if they were in themselves good questions. But they are not.
Let us take a few examples. The minister has asked whether Canadian development assistance should be directed only toward those countries which have achieved some yet undefined level of human rights. Does the minister believe that using our aid as a means of pressure on another nation to adopt these yet undefined standards is a practicable policy? If so, can she inform the House what are the criteria she would have Canada adopt in its development assistance program? How does she intend to apply those standards once they are defined? Does she foresee the sudden termination of Canadian aid if there is a change of government in a recipient country which brings a reversal in its earlier human rights practices? Does she believe, in any event, that threatening the withdrawal of Canadian assistance is going to intimidate wrongdoers? More important, does she really believe that such threats are in fact the most effective way of helping those who have been deprived of what Canadians may regard as human rights?
We could continue to query a policy which attempts to relate eligibility to Canadian aid to the vagaries of human rights practices across the Third World but perhaps, after all, the effort is unnecessary. In a sense the minister has answered her own questions, but in answering her question regarding aid and human rights she unfortunately did so with a statement which contradicts what she said earlier and merely serves to confuse further. I refer to the minister's statement at the United Nations that "development assistance does not imply the foisting of one country's social. . . philosophy on another". How does one square that statement with a policy to restrict Canadian aid only to those countries which adopt our social philosophy?
In mentioning human rights, I should not want the opportunity to pass without hearing from the minister about her apparently ill-fated proposal at the United Nations General Assembly to create the new office of under-secretary general for human rights. My understanding is that this Canadian proposal has now been withdrawn, only a few weeks after it was introduced. What happened? Had the government not done its homework in determining beforehand whether there was an adequate number of co-sponsors? Was it that the idea was so inchoate, so hastily conceived, that in this sensitive area where the internal affairs of sovereign nations are so jealously guarded, few other countries were ready to adopt this
November 14, 1979

approach to the complex and controversial question of human rights?
Allow me to return to the subject of Canada's development assistance by noting another series of questions which has inevitably led to yet more confusion and contradictions in Canadian external relations. In Toronto, the minister asked whether Canada should reverse its policy of the past years and now concentrate its aid on those developing countries which are nearing the stage of economic "take-off' or self-sustaining growth.
If in fact this represents a new government policy, the first thing to say about it is that, as in so many areas of international relations, we would presumably have other countries do as we do. Who, then, would be left to help the poorest countries where life, in the words of the president of the World Bank, is "a condition so degraded by disease, illiteracy, malnutrition and squalor as to deny its victims basic human necessities"? If Canada shifts the emphasis of assistance away from such countries, are we to console ourselves with the hope that someone else will help?
The second thing to say about a policy of helping only those countries on the threshold of self-sufficiency is that many of them are among the OPEC countries. Is it now the government's intention to direct our development assistance to OPEC countries to help push them over that threshold? Perhaps not, since those same OPEC countries would have been alienated by the government's hapless excursion into the Jerusalem problem. If it is not the government's intention to concentrate aid on the OPEC countries, perhaps it has in mind certain contries of Latin America, but the minister has expressed reservations about human rights in some of them, so perhaps they too are excluded. In any event, a policy of concentration upon "take-off' countries would mean abandoning many of our Commonwealth and Francophone friends. The minister gave additional substance to this impression by stating in Toronto that Africa is no longer an area of commitment for Canada.
Southern Africa remains one of the most inflammable areas of the world today. Canadians do not live in a fireproof house, if they ever did. Neither Canada nor her allies can simply turn their backs on southern Africa asking, as the minister did, "Who in Canada cares".
Even more fundamentally, Canadians are not more immune from their history than any other nation. We are one nation drawing upon the common heritage of the English and Frenchspeaking countries. That heritage finds expression in part in our external aid programs. Our links with the former British and French colonies are an expression of Canada's dual character. Are we to turn our back on that essential heritage? These links are not to be dismissed lightly. They are especially valuable in binding the world together with ties which transcend regional preoccupations or narrow self-interest.
One more word about Canada's development assistance. The size and nature of our commitment have recently been placed in real doubt by conflicting statements of the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and
Supply
the Minister of State for CIDA. The remarks made by the Minister of Finance in Belgrade in October were contradictory in themselves. While asserting that we want to narrow the gap between the industrialized nations and the developing world as quickly as possible and that our commitment to that goal is evidenced not only by our words but by our deeds, he added that further increases in the transfer of resources are difficult to justify to Canadians until our own economic situation improves. Our deeds, apparently, are going to be put off to a later date.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs herself has been vague on the question of how much support the government is prepared to give to development assistance. CIDA's budget as a percentage of our gross national product has continued to drop. It is now below the .5 per cent level, well below our stated goal of .7 per cent of gross national product devoted to official development assistance.
In spite of her promises to fight world poverty and to continue Canadian efforts in development, the minister will not give us deeds to bear out her words. The .7 per cent target remains in limbo. The Minister of State for CIDA recently refused to commit himself to this goal, or even to annual increments which would ensure that we would reach it.

speechtext:
I would like to advise the hon. member on certain matters he mentioned. He spoke about foreign policy. The last time that foreign policy was reviewed in this country was in 1970-71. That is the last time, and it was not reviewed as we are suggesting it be reviewed, with public input, with people being allowed to help formulate the foreign policy of their country by using a parliamentary committee so that people can come before it and make their views known, because I believe Canadians want to express points of view on foreign policy and that should be a vehicle for them through which to do it. That is why we are asking that this matter be dealt with by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence of this Parliament. I would hope that the hon. member would make it a point to try to contribute to that, but he should be aware of the fact that this was not done in that way in the previous Liberal era because there was no means by which public input could be provided. Policy was developed from the top down only, and we do not believe in that sort of approach. 1 will give the hon. member an example so that he will know exactly why I say this.
The hon. member has made reference to the lack of policy statements or activities. Since this government assumed office in May we made some very important statements with regard to policy and they related particularly to our approach to the refugee situation. With regard to our strategy in Southeast Asia, we put forward a proposal to provide places of resettlement in this country for refugees from Southeast Asia and we did it by proposing a method by which Canadians could share with their government by participation. Canadians have shown since then that they wanted to contribute and to help in the resettlement of some 50,000 refugees from Southeast Asia. And what did the Leader of the Opposition call it? He called it a cop-out, because he does not know anything about Canadian people sharing with their government in reaching policy decisions. That is why we put forward the proposal of using the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence as the proper means for allowing individual Canadians, groups and organizations, to help formulate the policy for the 1980s. We consider it an ongoing way in which this

government has shown by example that it wants Canadians involved. It wants them involved in raising the visibility of foreign policy in this country.
I would like to reply now, Mr. Chairman, to a couple of other comments that the hon. member has made. I suppose I should not say he made a gratuitous statement, but nevertheless he made the rather unique statement that the minister stands still. I want to tell him that he is the only person I know in this country who thinks that I have been standing still since the election.
