I tend, therefore, to try to be practical in those matters of international relations. 1 must say that my concerns are economic in nature; I care very much about the economic and industrial situation in this country. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, I have some moral misgivings. 1 consider myself as pure as anyone else, as well-intentioned as anyone else, and wonder simply, perhaps banally, on behalf of the people of Canada, whether it might not be possible to reconcile both interests better than we now do, whether it might not be possible to conduct highly sophisticated, moral and respected politics abroad without damaging our trade interests too much.
That, I believe, is an honest concern. If the minister tells me that there are situations in which Canada should sacrifice its economic interests to superior moral interests, I shall be the first to approve. But what displeases me, in fact distresses me, is when I see the government harming the economy of my country for reasons which may seem moral but which, in fact, are not, and which may even not be in the greatest interest of
Supply
the country they are supposed to help, or which are not even achievable. 1 am interested in that balance between objectives, and that is precisely what I should like to get the minister to reflect upon. 1 know she has done so previously, but I trust she will do so even more and in greater depth now.
The example to give here is, naturally, that of Jerusalem, more specifically the plan to transfer our embassy from Tel-Aviv to Jerusalem. That is a typical example of the use of a seemingly moral concern for reasons which were not very moral. And I am not being uncharitable when I say that. No Prime Minister has ever done so much, in so little time, to harm the trade position of his country, in one specific area of the world, for so mean a purpose, namely that of getting two of his candidates elected in the Toronto area.
Besides, it is not up to me to rap the fingers of the minister in that regard. Mr. Stanfield has already done that in a rather remarkable way, and if I wanted to be mean 1 would read into Hansard the admonitions Mr. Stanfield gave the government. Before embarking on a crusade, the minister should ask herself if it is a worth-while crusade, and we should ask ourselves if we are truly helping the country we are supposed to be helping. Perhaps she should show some moderation in her good feelings, which are well known.
I am done with the Jerusalem issue. Despite my admiration for the major issues involved in that project, I have no admiration whatsoever for the way the government proceeded. I deeply regret the embarrassment, the problems, the damages that this adventure caused Canadian businessmen who had been working in that area for many years, who had invested thousands of dollars and who got the wind taken out of their sails by a government that is supposed to help them.
This tendency to moralize is deeply ingrained in my hon. friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In an interview, which may have been misquoted and which she granted to John Walker of Southam Press, she apparently said, and I quote:

As to where she draws the line between moral judgments and trade, say in Candu reactors, in the light of her desire for "the most stringent conditions possible" in nuclear safeguards, MacDonald said:
"I'm not prepared to do that at present. I'm raising this because I don't want to give anybody the answer, or what I think is my answer, before the discussion gets well under way."
The minister likes this kind of question. She goes to the United Nations talking about nuclear reactors and says the following:
We demand that stringent safeguards be applied by countries buying Canadian nuclear power facilities or materials.... We want to ensure that the continued recourse to nuclear power is undertaken in the most stringent conditions possible-
I cannot disagree with philosophy, theology, morality, ethics and so on. I am just saying that my hon. friend should be most cautious. I am not lecturing the minister, but if she is not yet sufficiently aware, she should be made aware that every one of these statements creates uneasiness. People say, "What does

November 14, 1979
Supply
she mean? Does she mean that from now on agreements signed by Canada on nuclear safeguards might be subjected to a rule of unilaterally imposed retroactivity? Does she mean that?"

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is what you say.

No. I am just wondering what it means. A lot of people around the world wonder what it means. The world is a strange place; international trade is difficult. I had the good fortune of working at it for three years. It is terribly difficult. When the minister feels inclined to make a moral statement to impress Canada and the world, I want her to please think about those guys who are trying to sell something around the world and might be embarrassed by her statement. If the good reputation of Canada is involved, the statement should be made, but the minister should not make it simply to raise an issue. The minister should not raise issues just for the purpose of starting interesting debates. Trading internationally is very difficult, I repeat. Those who have done so know how difficult it is. I used to say that the great difficulty with international trade is that it is done outside of Canada!
This afternoon the minister raised the following question, and I think I have it right: Why should we give aid to countries where violent abuse of human rights takes place? On the face of it, the answer appears simple; certainly not. But let us think about it a bit more. Who violates these rights? It is the governments of those countries. What is the relationship, in many instances, between the governments of those countries and the people of those countries?
None.

Very often the people made no contribution at all in the selection of those leaders. So for a very good purpose, punishing or preventing governments that violate human rights, my hon. friend would, strangely enough, punish people for the sins of their leaders, when they had hardly anything, if anything at all, to say about their selection. Those are my preoccupations and I just wanted to share them with my hon. friend.
Similarly, on the subject of aid, she has raised a problem that is intellectually fascinating. Who is it that Canada should help? Should we go for the poor, the poorest of the poor, the richest of the poor? Universities rightly delight in provoking debates of this kind. I wonder, and this is a question, not a lecture, to what extent it is practical for a government to do it. My knowledge is that countries receiving aid are of many types, of many categories. Some need certain types of aid that are completely different from the types of aid needed by other countries.
As the minister knows, I used to be a great defender of the idea that Canada had to support, by way of aid, countries that had the means for their economic development. I was very strong on the subject and I carried a list of these countries at the time. Why? Simply because we are partly in this game to

expand Canadian trade abroad. There is no shame in that. If we are ashamed of that we are in trouble indeed.
A number of countries have the means of their industrial development. They are on the verge of it, they are on their way to it, and it is quite desirable for Canada to help them in certain types of ways. What will be needed there will be sophisticated equipment, engineering services, and financing. Other countries, the poorest of the poor, will need an entirely different kind of aid, teachers, nurses, technicians. What I would like to see the minister address herself to is exactly that; not a philosophical debate on whom we should help, or who needs the most; but by what means can we help a particular type of country, by what means can we help another type of country, and this to me is much more satisfactory and realistic than a major discussion on whom we should help.
Dealing with nuclear reactors, I consider that to be a good and decent Canadian export. The Financial Post said the other day that if you want to have a nuclear policy, first of all you are going to have to decide if you want to sell and, secondly, to whom and, thirdly, under what conditions. I suggest that this is not a thought to be ignored. On this subject I am afraid, particularly in view of the minister's statement which she is going to explain in a moment, and particularly in view of the committee that is going to be created to look into the whole Canadian nuclear policy including exports, I am afraid, to speak like my friend, the Minister of State for International Trade, that we are again going to have a "hiatus" in marketing that product while we study the subject.
It seems to me that the only way to counter this is by the minister here this afternoon getting up and saying to us that she is very much in favour of the sale of nuclear reactors under certain types of conditions. I hope that while she makes these conditions very demanding she will not go to the extent of making them impossible, because we might then end up in a situation as we apparently are in with Argentina, where the country that got the contract is offering the safeguards that we were willing to accept in the first place.
The general subject of my remarks was really the relationship between diplomacy and trade and, much as I would like to state that I recognize the importance of ethical standards and moral objectives, I would like on behalf of Canadian workers and Canadian businessmen to ask that more attention should be given to rather down to earth considerations like the economic wealth and the economic state of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member finished on a note of throwing into question the values of ethical standards and moral behaviour. I would trust that in throwing them into question he does not intend to abandon them.
No, and I said so specifically.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I would hope that we would still, as a country, be able to exhibit both ethical standards and moral behaviour in all our activities, whether in trade, in aid, in external negotiations or whatever we might do. I want to thank the hon. member for the suggestions he has made. I would
November 14, 1979

hope that he would see his way possible to become a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence because, from his experience, he will be able to contribute greatly to the review process that will shortly be under way.
There are only two matters that I would like to address that he has brought up at the present time. One has to do with the comments I have made at the United Nations with regard to the most stringent standards that we would want to see placed on the sales, or on the question of nuclear proliferation.
I had said that Canada abides by having the most stringent safeguards possible and that we look forward as well to the results of the International Nuclear Fuel Cycle Evaluation, 1NFCE, which will probably be available to us in February of next year; a study which was undertaken by some 45 countries, which was joined in by the previous government, and whose objective it was to make the whole question of the nuclear fuel cycle more proliferation proof. Therefore, I have reiterated certainly what had been our party's stand in opposition and what is the government's stand at the present time, and what I thought was the position of the former government, that it too adhered to trying to accomplish for the safety of the world the most stringent safeguards possible. I would hope that the hon. gentleman's party is not moving away from that position, because that would be a disastrous thing if Canada, one of the leading countries in this discussion over the years, and one of the countries which has tried to state to the world its belief in full scope safeguards, should in any way feel that that standard should be diminished.
The hon. member had raised that matter in connection with comments that I had made, and he, as well, raised it with regard to Argentina and what was happening with regard to sales to Argentina. I am sure he will be well aware that, under pressure from the opposition, under pressure from many groups, under pressure from world opinion, the former government re-evaluated its stand, its nuclear safeguards, and upgraded them during the time that that government was in discussion with Argentina about nuclear sales. 1 am sure he realizes that that was done. It was a step that we, as members of the opposition, applauded.
I want to draw to the attention of the hon. member what my predecessor said at the time those standards were upgraded by the previous government when he spoke on this very subject in the House on December 22, 1976. The former minister was making a statement about nuclear safeguards and about nuclear sales abroad. As it is reported in Hansard at page 2256 on that date, the former minister said:
It is for this reason that the Government of Canada has unilaterally decided to strengthen further Canada's safeguard requirements. As in the past we are prepared to accept the commercial consequences of being clearly ahead of other suppliers. This is the price we are prepared to pay to curb the threat to mankind of nuclear proliferation.
1 trust that that statement was made on behalf of the government and is a statement in which those now in opposition will continue to believe.

The hon. member has raised the question of human rights again and made reference to something I said earlier this afternoon when I talked about countries that violently abuse human rights, and our aid relations with them. I mentioned a specific country, Vietnam. That is the country to which I had referred, but I want the hon. member to know that the cessation of aid to Vietnam-which I applauded-was taken by the former government, by the party in which the hon. member now sits. I agreed with that decision, and I will continue to agree with actions of that kind. I would hope that in opposition the members who once sat on this side and who have had a long-time association with that party are not suddenly reversing their positions, which I felt they had taken because of their beliefs in ethical and moral behaviour, and that they will not be backing away from these beliefs at this time.

1 would like to begin my intervention with a little comment made without any malice. A while ago, the minister took a rather shabby attitude towards my colleague from Etobicoke North, which she does not usually do but it should be noted that we have now been discussing for an hour the points that he has raised. I therefore suppose that the minister recognizes the relevance of his questions and I hope that in the future she will be above partisanship and will do her best to meet the concerns, which 1 know to be sincere, of my colleague from Etobicoke North who, it should be noted, served for 12 years in the Department of External Affairs, the department of the hon. member opposite to whom I address my comments, and I think that after 12 years in this field we can assume that he has at least as much experience as the minister and myself.
Having said this, Mr. Chairman, I would like to associate myself with the comments made by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton and urge the minister to avoid falling into the Kantian philosophy of categories in the international forums which she addresses and where she has spoken several times in the last six months. Reality is not always black and white. There are sometimes grey areas and I believe that this is what the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton meant earlier when he deplored the fact that the minister had raised debatable issues without necessarily providing solutions.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that we shall have the opportunity to hold such debates in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence when the minister decides to refer these matters to the committee, and it will be very healthy for us to hold such a debate in Canada on all the issues that she has raised concerning morality, aid, and our philosophy in external relations whether in relation to foreign aid or to bilateral or multilateral discussions.
But at the international level surely the minister knows that the touchiness of the nations which gather for those conferences, their excessive, extreme, sometimes justified, sometimes

November 14, 1979
Supply
unjustified touchiness goes against their good intentions and this I do not contest. She will certainly remember the letter I sent her at the beginning of her mandate to congratulate her for her position in Geneva where she censured Vietnam as a nation that did not really try to help its people. 1 maintain my support of the minister.
Elowever, it is always dangerous in international forums or before an assembly of the nations to raise issues which do not call for easy answers, for the countries to which those questions are put always find it embarrassing to answer. And often it just creates more problems for Canada-the good intentions of Premier Lougheed notwithstanding-rather than solving them. So, I join my colleague from Ottawa-Carleton in urging the minister to curb her enthusiasm and maybe redirect it to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence when we shall have the opportunity to discuss these issues in depth.
Now, 1 wish to ask the minister more specific questions which are still perfectly pertinent unfortunately as they refer to the hostage-taking incident in the United States embassy in Tehran. The minister had the opportunity to answer some questions put by my colleagues on this side of the House about the safety of Canadian citizens in Iran and I wish to ask the following questions: three questions to which she might answer and then I might deal with another subject.
The Iranian foreign minister-we do not know whether or not there still is a civil government but we suppose there still is a foreign affairs minister-has recently met with all members of the diplomatic corps to transmit a request from the government of Iran to put pressure on the government of the United States, more particularly on President Carter to force him to give in to the demands of the extremist students who are now holding the United States embassy in Tehran, and presumably send the Shah back to Iran-we do not know whether he would be extradited to Iran or to some other country.
First, did the the ambassador of Canada in Iran attend this meeting early this week, I think, and second did he transmit to the Iranian authorities the wish unanimously expressed in this House that the hostages be liberated forthwith without any conditions? Moreover, did he tell the Iranian authorities about the wave of indignation that this unacceptable act of terrorism created in Canada?
Third, earlier this week the Government of Canada offered its good offices to the American government to help it solve the crisis. What do these good offices amount to? Do they amount only to consular services to the American nationals in Iran or do they go beyond these simple services eventually to encompass direct political intervention?
Fourth, the government of Iran recently announced-I think it was yesterday-its intention to appeal to the Security Council to discuss the matter. Does the Government of Canada- which 1 know is not a member of the Security Council-intend

to exert unofficial pressure on the Security Council so that the inalienable principles which are, on the one hand, the right of political asylum, and on the other hand, diplomatic immunity in a foreign country, are duly taken into consideration by the Security Council?
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister might answer now and then I could go on to the second part of my questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the participation of the hon. member.

I will take the questions that he has posed, directly, if I may.
First he asked whether our ambassador was present at the meeting in Iran to which most of the representatives of foreign nations had been summoned by the foreign minister of Iran. Yes, Mr. Chairman, he was present at that meeting.
Second, the hon. member asked whether we had communicated to the Iranian government-if we can call it that- the protest made here in this House of Commons and our protest as a government. We did that directly through the charges d'affaires in the Iranian embassy. That was communicated, I presume, to the revolutionary council or whatever is operating in Iran in the way of a government.
The third question he asked was whether our willingness to be of assistance to the United States had been made known and what kind of assistance it would be. Certainly, that means consular assistance to those Americans who would be without an embassy at the present time.
I should like the hon. member to know that the offer of assistance was conveyed not only through our ambassador in Iran but that I spoke directly to Secretary of State Vance and informed him of Canada's willingness to be of assistance in any way that the United States thought we could help in this very intense situation. He expressed his appreciation for that.
Coming to the last question about the Security Council, I might say that when I spoke to Secretary of State Vance for the second time today, when he was in New York to attend sessions of the Security Council, I again offered our assistance, in any way that we could, to try to resolve what is a very desperate situation.

I thank the minister for her explanations. Once again, at the risk of being paternalistic, I would urge the minister to be excessively careful about that very legitimate offer she made to the U.S. government, because some countries could eventually interpret that move as an interference, an intrusion in internal affairs, but 1 am sure the minister wants her officials to act with due consideration.
Now, I would like to touch on another subject I discussed with the minister in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, Canadian assistance to Cambodian refugees. I must say that Canada has done more than
November 14, 1979

its share to help Vietnamese refugees by allowing a great many of them to come to Canada. I believe it is the best effort in international co-operation we have seen in Canada during the last decade, even though Cambodia is now the scene of a tragedy which results in quite complex material problems. The international community held a meeting, I believe, early last week-I wanted to be there but because of the division which took place here I could not go to New York with the minister. Sometimes the procedure in this Elouse is a diriment impediment against one's best wishes and best intentions. Those technical problems are very important because there are in fact two Cambodian governments, at least as far as the international community is concerned, two Cambodian governments, one de jure and one de facto government, if I may put it like that. The Kampuchean government put in place by the Vietnamese government refused until recently to collaborate actively in the delivery of the enormous assistance that the international community intends to give to the Cambodian refugees in Cambodia. There again we should differentiate- as the minister pointed out-between two problems, first, the refugees living in Cambodia and second the refugees who are now in the vicinity of the border between Cambodia and Thailand and in Thailand itself. The minister announced that the Canadian government has tripled its food assistance, especially to Cambodians, but she could not answer me when I asked her whether or not the Cambodian government was willing to collaborate to transport those food supplies to the regions where the situation is most critical.
I think that members of the American Congress are about to leave or have already left for Phnom Penh to discuss with the Cambodian government the question of channelling assistance to Cambodians. In view of that, can the minister assure the House that the assistance Canada generously committed itself to give during the international conference last week, will actually reach the Cambodian refugees who badly need it, that it will reach those living close to the battlefields? Does the Kampuchean government now intend to co-operate with the international community to deliver that assistance, what is exactly the nature of the assistance that Canada is directing to Thailand to help that country solve the problem of Cambodian refugees coming in, and fourth, given that the minister is certainly aware of the fact that a group of volunteer doctors have in recent months accomplished tremendous work in Hong Kong camps and now want to go further and to reach the border zone of Thailand, is it the intention of the government to supply technical and financial help to those willing Canadians, to those doctors who are now in the field doing their best to lessen the terrible sufferings which are the lot of so many Cambodians now?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first may I just say that I should like to reassure the hon. member that in conveying our offer of assistance to the United States, it was done in a
Supply
humanitarian fashion to assist those people who are without any consular services at the present time.
With regard to the situation in Kampuchea, the hon. member has noted that we have tripled our aid since the time I appeared before the committee and talked about a $5 million contribution to the appeal that the Secretary General had made for aid to Kampuchea. We have tripled that from $5 million to $15 million. We have made that aid available to the international agencies which are best equipped to handle the situation in Kampuchea, in our view, that is, to the International Red Cross and to UNICEF, which have the basic organization that will enable them to distribute the food aid, medical supplies and clothing to those who have been so hurt by this tragedy.
When listening to the news this morning, particularly that from the United States, I heard that relief planes are landing in Phnom Penh. We were assured that the supplies they carried were distributed to all of the refugees, to Kampucheans throughout the country. One has to take into consideration the lack of infrastructure there at the present time.
With regard to Canadian involvement in this, we have indicated that we want our aid to go to Kampuchea directly, regardless of the struggle between the Pol Pot regime and the present Heng Samrin regime. As far as possible, we want it to be distributed throughout Kampuchea. We also want to make sure that some is earmarked for the frontier camps in Thailand. As far as the actual physical arrangements of that distribution are concerned, we are leaving this up to these major non-governmental organizations.
I wish to inform the hon. member that our director in CIDA for the non-governmental organizations is going to Kampuchea personally to take a look at the situation and to advise our government on how he sizes up the relief operation that is under way. On his return we will be in communication with the International Red Cross, UNICEF and the United Nations Commissioner for Refugees.
I will only be 20 seconds, Mr. Chairman. May 1 suggest to the minister that this report be made available to the House and interested members?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will be delighted to do that.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure the minister that I do not intend to subject her or the committee to a long lecture or to a display of detailed knowledge on certain matters which most people know anyway, but to ask some deliberate questions. One goes back to the question raised by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood in the general area of southern Africa. I believe the minister said that a request for elements from Canada to supervise elections in Zimbabwe-Rhodesia had not been received. That is quite understandable.

November 14, 1979
Supply
1 wonder if, in the conversations that have been going on, to which 1 am sure the minister and the department are privy, the supervisors of these elections that are expected will be uniformed personnel, civilian personnel drawn from the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, or in the nature of police. This applies just not in Zimbabwe Rhodesia but in the United Nations supervised elections that are likely to take place in Namibia, South West Africa. I realize these are different sorts of questions. I just wonder what sort of personnel are being sent. I also have a further question on southern Africa.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to participation in any internationally acceptable force that would help out in the transition period in Zimbabwe Rhodesia, we would have to await the request from the British government. We have not been informed as to the kind of force that would be required in that situation. We have made it known, as I mentioned at Lusaka, that we would be prepared to take part in trying to come to some internationally acceptable solution in that part of the world, and that meant as far as we were concerned on that point, helping to monitor the election processes. However, we would have to await the specific request from the British government before making any definitive reply.
We are not now trying to say we would be prepared to send peacekeeping troops or to send police when what might be asked for would be people who specialize in election procedures. That was how the discussion initially came about in Lusaka. Therefore, we would await that request, if it were to be forthcoming.
The second area the hon. member mentioned was with regard to Namibia. 1 would think any request in that regard is further down the road than a request for assistance for Zimbabwe Rhodesia. I mention that because at this very moment there are discussions going on in Geneva, under the aegis of the Secretary General, in which the Group of Five, of which Canada is one, is involved along with South Africa, representatives of SWAPO, and the internal group within Namibia. Those discussions will be getting under way this week. Therefore, there will still be a lengthy number of discussions that have to take place before any special formula will be arrived at as to how elections are carried out in Namibia.

There must have been some thinking in the Department of External Affairs on the supervision of elections, which is the matter at issue, as to whether it would be uniformed personnel, in military uniforms or police uniforms, or civilians, if Canada has made an offer. Surely someone has thought where this group of people will be found. If we are suddenly asked for returning officers, is it possible to recruit experienced returning officers? 1 am just wondering if there has been any thought about that in the department. I agree the question has not been put specifically, but I hope that some thought has been given to this matter.
To go back to Rhodesia for a second, I have just received a copy of the report of the Department of External Affairs. 1 have glanced through parts of it. That part dealing with southern Africa deals with the Zimbabwe Rhodesia situation.
It says that the security situation in that area had deteriorated to such a point that martial law had been imposed and that many whites were leaving the country.
A couple of paragraphs further on it states with respect to Zambia that the country's front line position vis-a-vis Rhodesia made it a target of land and air attacks. I see no mention in this report of land attacks in Rhodesia itself by the so-called liberation force. The reasons for the deterioration of the situation in Rhodesia were surely brought about by the attacks from front line states to which I believe the Canadian government, through some of the NGOs, has been contributing support. I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to make some comments on that.
With regard to South Africa itself, on page 84, and it is true we are talking about 1978, 1 notice there is no indication that the South African government intended to depart from the essential features of its apartheid policy. I also wish to refer to the following paragraph on page 84, in the middle of the page. Then there was the announcement by the former government that South African sportsmen and sports officials would henceforth be denied Canadian visas. I am wondering whether any representations have been made to the minister or whether the department has received any representations from the South African representatives in this country, or whether the department has received reports from our ambassador in South Africa as to changes in the sports policy of the South African government. Does that ban on sportsmen and sports officials still stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the question of the kind of force or group which might be requested by the British government to assist in the transitional period, in the election period in Zimbabwe Rhodesia, it is difficult to give the hon. member any details at this point because we simply do not know the nature of the request. As the Prime Minister said the other day during his press conference, he would want to consider the nature of such a request before making any statement on it. We have indicated our willingness to play a part in seeing the election process properly carried out, but we do not know the kind of role the British government would envisage for other members of the Commonwealth or, possibly, for countries outside the Commonwealth.
With regard to the annual review to which the hon. member referred, he will note that it is the annual review for 1978 and that it was prepared in a period prior to my assuming my present portfolio. It is not something in whose preparation I was involved. As to his comments about front line states, activities of other groups, and so on, I will take note of them and take them into consideration. I can assure him that in the discussions to which we were privy-and I say "we" as meaning members of the government who attended the Commonwealth conference in Lusaka-we were tremendously impressed by the contributions made by the presidents of the front line states, Mr. Nyerere and Mr. Kaunda. Throughout this period from July onward when the Prime Minister and my

November 14, 1979

department have been in touch with them, they have been exceedingly helpful in trying to move toward a resolution of this problem, and I want to commend them for that.
1 believe the hon. member mentioned that there had been some support given to military intervention-was it military intervention?
Through NGOs.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There was no support of that nature provided by CIDA. None whatsoever. Again I should like to stress that it is humanitarian and relief activities only which have been assisted by CIDA through the non-governmental organizations.
I myself had an opportunity to see some of those programs in action in Zambia when I visited victory camps in which CUSO is doing some work helping out in a situation where some 8,000 women and children are housed in a camp for refugees. CUSO had helped with the building of houses, the installation of facilities and so on. These are people who have been uprooted, who are separated from their homes, separated from husbands, from male partners. For the most part they are working in a situation where, through the assistance of international non-governmental organizations, they create industries in which they are engaged, are turning out clothing both for other refugees and for sale to help themselves Financially. They are now getting a very good operation going there. A lot of that initially was made possible with the help of the CUSO people in the region.
As to the question with regard to South Africa, the hon. member asked whether there had been any request from South Africa with regard to changes in the policy concerning sports throughout the world. I would inform him there has been no request of which I am aware communicated to my department.
Or information from South Africa with respect to this?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, I am not aware of any information which has been communicated in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, Canada is a responsible member of the international community and we have proven that at all sessions of the Law of the Sea Conference. The Canadian delegation is one of the best equipped under the skilful direction of His Excellency Ambassador Allan Beesley. It has always proudly borne the Canadian flag and must continue to uphold the interest of all Canadians for generations to come. The government must continue to provide the Canadian delegation with funds to hire experts and resource staff. At the tenth session, we must not be outdone by the United States, the U.S.S.R. or Japan. Several important items for Canada will again be on the agenda at the tenth session to be held in
Supply
New York and Geneva in 1980. To name just two, the issues of territorial economic fishing zones and the development of offshore mineral resources will again come up.
Mr. Chairman, Canada has proposed to set a limit to the development of nodules so as not to endanger nickel mines in Canada, more particularly those in Sudbury. Japan, the U.S.S.R., the United States and members of the European Community interested in the development of nodules do not want to hear anything about a limit being set. Those countries which are the biggest consumers in the world will become suppliers, and that would threaten the mining industry as we know it in Canada.
Our Canadian delegation must continue to promote the idea of a 200-mile economic zone and have our 200-mile fishing zone accepted internationally. Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister is aware that the United States are not particularly in favour of those 200-mile zones. The Canadian delegation at the Law of the Sea Conference was behind a majority of the proposals contained in the working paper that will one day become the Law of the Sea Treaty. Supported by the former government, our delegates were able to choose their own friends without making enemies. Relations are excellent with the Group of Seventy-seven as well as with industrialized countries.
The minister is certainly aware that Canada's main objectives at the Law of the Sea Conference are, to mention but a few, the protection of the environment along our coastlines and in fishing areas, the protection of resources on the continental shelf, the setting of a limit on the development of seabed resources, that is, undersea mining resources, the protection of our renewable resources, such as the Atlantic and Pacific salmon, and the delimitation of our fishing, territorial and economic zones.
After this short enumeration, Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct two questions to the minister. First of all, what diplomatic offensive does she intend to start within the next few months to make sure that the Canadian delegation obtains the expected success at the tenth conference? And then, will the budget cuts forecast by the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board directly affect the Canadian delegation, forcing it to do without part of its staff? The budget cuts must not weaken the Canadian delegation at the Law of the Sea Conference.
The problems discussed at the international conference are not all black or all white, as my colleague just said; they cover a variety of colours. The Canadian delegation must have experts ever ready to take part in the debate and Canada has a significant role to play at this tenth session of the conference on the Law of the Sea.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for his remarks this afternoon because I am fully aware of the importance of the Law of the Sea.

Throughout his time here and in various sessions of the Law of the Sea Conference over the past ten years, the hon. member has made a very significant contribution to the developments which have taken place, and we on this side of the Elouse are very aware of that.
I would like to tell him that the urgency which is now attached to this is of very real importance to the government because we know that we are now in the final stages of the Law of the Sea negotiations. We are down to trying to negotiate the last 5 per cent to 10 per cent of the agreements, and we know that these have to be arrived at in the next two meetings. They have to be settled within this coming year at the two meetings which will be held in March and, later, in June.
The difficulty which would be faced by those who have been engaged in this exercise over the past ten years is that if those final and most difficult items cannot be resolved-such as the one referred to by the hon. member, the ceiling with regard to nickel production in the seabed-everything we have decided on previously would be endangered. All of the agreements and all of the measures which have already been put in place as part of the total package which will come out after the ten-year period could indeed be jeopardized. I am talking about things like the agreements which were arrived at which would greatly benefit Canada with regard to pollution in the Arctic, or the agreements which were arrived at on the extension to the 200-mile limit. All of these things are part of the total package, and therefore it is absolutely vital that we resolve in this last six-month to nine-month period of operation the few outstanding items, so that the previous ones already in place will not be jeopardized.
1 want to tell the hon. member that under the chairmanship of Ambassador Beesley, to whom the hon. member has referred and the work he has done throughout this lengthy period, we will be taking steps to try to resolve the difficulties which still exist on these outstanding matters, whether with the United States or with other countries.
We will be attaching the very highest priority to this because, as I mentioned, we know what we would lose if we do not get those last few items locked into place.
Therefore there would be no question as to either the quality or quantity of the delegation, the people who are involved in this, being reduced in what I hope will be the last few months before the final solution is reached.

Mr. Speaker, this being my first opportunity to exchange ideas with the minister, I would like first of all to congratulate her on her nomination. In fact I was very happy,
and I say that in all sincerity, when in June last I heard that the Prime Minister had appointed her to that office. I think the minister possesses the high-mindedness, the open-mindedness and also the capacity to keep herself above political partisanship to fill such an important office, and knowing her extremely liberal record I know that sometimes she will feel, alas, isolated within cabinet and her party caucus, but she can count on our support.
Of course time is running short, and 1 would have liked to deal most particularly with the speech she made at the General Assembly of the United Nations last September 25, a speech which struck me because of what she said and what she did not
say.
Let us start with what she did not say. 1 would like the minister to explain in the few minutes we have left how she managed the feat of addressing the General Assembly of the United Nations without saying anything about the situation in the Middle East, the powder keg in the world that is most likely to blow up. I fear that, following the regrettable and foolish decision of her leader to move the Canadian embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, which the government reversed to the greatest relief of us all, she found herself in such an embarrassing situation that she chose to avoid the subject.
1 would ask her to say exactly, and 1 now come to what she said as opposed to what she did not say, what has been done about her recommendation, her most laudable suggestion that proceeded from extremely commendable reasons, that the position of assistant undersecretary in charge of human rights be established? Has Canada taken some initiatives to further that proposal? And finally, considering her interest in human rights, the main topic of her speech, I think, would the minister say whether the government made in the last few days or will make representations to have the Israeli government free the mayor of Nablus, Mr. Bassam Shakaa, and abandon its intention of deporting him from Jordan? It is obvious to me that it is a matter related to human rights.

Indeed, 1 did not raise the Middle East issue nor did 1 talk about the U.S.S.R. and our alliance with the European countries.
